newsitem.title: USA: Chase sees Dow at 7000 in '97, T-bond yields up.
newsitem.headline: Chase sees Dow at 7000 in '97, T-bond yields up.

text.p: The Dow Jones Industrial Average should edge up to 7000 by the end of 1997, with U.S. Treasury 30-year bond yields climbing to 6.75 percent sometime in the year, economists for Chase Manhattan Private Bank N.A. predicted Tuesday.
Overall, the U.S. economy should continue to grow at a slightly slower rate next year, said Chase chief market analyst Donald Fine and chief investment officer Henry Goss.
At 1210 EST/1710 GMT, the Dow Industrials were up 32.79 at 6496.73. The benchmark T-bond was yielding 6.49 percent.
"We seem to be in the perfect world," Fine said at Chase's annual economic outlook breakfast. "While the economy is slowing down, it is not going to stop."

He predicted GDP growth rould rise in fourth quarter 1996 on the strength of "a good Christmas," then slow to 1.5 percent in early 1997. Inflation should creep up to 3.2 percent to 3.5 percent next year, he said.

"Capital spending is still strong," Fine said. It will slow next year but, "It'll still probably be the strength component of the GDP. The industrial sector is fine. It's not booming. It's not slowing."
As aging baby boomers increasingly plan for retirement, savings and 401K investments will grow. That should help keep spending, inflation and interest rates low, he said.
However, if the economy slows more than expected next year, there will not be a backlog of unfilled orders to keep the labor market strong as there was when the last slowdown began in 1989.
As a result, Fine said, "The Fed wil react more quickly."
Fine, an adviser to the Federal Reserve, said the Fed is now "on hold."
"The market is priced exactly where the fed would like to see it. But remember, the fed has a bias toward tightening," Fine said.
He said Fedeal Reserve Chairman Greenspan's speech last week, in which he questioned whether there was unfounded exuberance in the stock market, was "chosen precisely to calm the market down."
Although stocks generally regained the losses they saw after that remark, "Just think of where we'd be without the comment," Fine said.
He and Goss said the equities market is fully valued but not overvalued.
Goss predicted operating earnings growth for the Standard & Poor's 500 would be between six percent and eight percent in 1997 versus eight to 10 percent projected for 1996.
He predicted prices for the S&P 500 would average 18.2 times forecast earnings for 1997, compared with 19.5 times projected earnings currently.

"Can valuations rise further? Probably not much further without becoming excessive," Goss said. "We're looking for further but modest gains in 1997. Are there speculative excesses within the market? We don't see a lot."

Goss said it may be time to realize some profits the U.S. equities market and diversify more into international equities. Specifically, Germany, Italy, France and Holland are beginning to adopt the efficiencies and agressive management that U.S. and British companies have already seen, he said.
"If I were starting to invest offshore, I would start to look at the major European countries," Goss said.
Chase Manhattan Private Bank is a unit of Chase Manhattan Corp. The private bank unit handles investment portfolios of "high net worth individuals," according to the economists.
